# A concave volume-quantile lift for every nonvertical cap direction

Let C be a compact convex body in R^n x R^d, d>=1. Write K_z for its
real-base fiber, P=projection(C), and r(z)=|K_z|^(1/d), where |.| is
d-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Fix an affine functional

    L(z,x)=a dot z+u dot x-b,   u!=0.

This note gives exact functional identities, not a new depth lower bound.
All integer-fiber sums below are finite. It does not replace them by a
real-base integral.

## 1. The joint concave inverse of cap-volume roots

For z in P and 0<=t<=r(z), define

    U(z,0)=max_(x in K_z)L(z,x),
    U(z,t)=sup{s:|K_z intersect {L(z,.)>=s}|>=t^d},   t>0.

The domain D={(z,t):z in P,0<=t<=r(z)} is convex. The function U is
finite, bounded by the minimum and maximum of L on C, upper semicontinuous,
and jointly concave on D.

To prove this including t=0, its hypograph is exactly the set of triples
(z,t,s) for which t>=0 and the cap

    A_(z,s)=K_z intersect {L(z,.)>=s}

is NONEMPTY and has volume at least t^d. The nonempty condition is essential
at t=0: empty caps do not define points of this hypograph. Minkowski
averages of any two such caps are contained in the corresponding cap at
the averaged z and s. The Brunn--Minkowski inequality, including a
nonempty zero-volume cap, gives the required averaged t. Hence this set
is convex. It is closed: along convergent parameters, nonempty caps have
points in a common compact set, so the limiting cap is nonempty; the
limsup of their volumes is bounded by the volume of the limiting cap,
using decreasing compact neighborhoods of that cap. This also proves
upper semicontinuity. Its projection is D, and its vertical sections are
the stated hypographs. Finiteness and boundedness follow from bounded L
on C. These facts prove every assertion about U and its domain.

For a positive-volume fiber, the cap-volume function is continuous and
strictly decreasing between the minimum and maximum of L on that fiber.
Continuity follows because u!=0 and each level hyperplane has zero
d-volume. Strict decrease follows because any interior subinterval of
the projection of a full-dimensional convex body has a positive-volume
preimage. Thus the inverse in the definition is unambiguous, with
U(z,r(z)) equal to the minimum of L on K_z.

## 2. Exact fiber moments and cap masses

On every positive-volume fiber,

    integral_(K_z) L(z,x) dx
       =d integral_0^(r(z)) t^(d-1) U(z,t) dt.         (1)

Indeed, the normalized cap survival function evaluated at L of a uniform
point is uniform on [0,1], by the preceding strict continuous inverse.
Integrating that inverse and substituting v=t^d/|K_z| proves (1).
All integrands are bounded; no unbounded-moment passage is involved.

For the closed cap H={L>=0}, define

    c_z=|K_z intersect H_z|^(1/d).

Its exact mass is c_z^d. If 0<c_z<r(z), it is the unique root of
U(z,c_z)=0. If the cap has zero volume, c_z=0; if it has full volume,
c_z=r(z). The values U(z,0) and U(z,r(z)) determine these endpoint
alternatives, including equality. A nonvertical boundary has zero
d-volume in each positive fiber, so all formulas concern the specified
CLOSED cap without a change in measured mass. The total mixed cap mass is

    sum_(z integer) c_z^d.                            (2)

On the projection of the nonempty convex set C intersect H, the cap roots
c(z) are concave by Brunn--Minkowski. No concavity is asserted after an
artificial zero extension outside that projection.

## 3. True-centroid and stationary-cap centering laws

Suppose the actual mixed centroid is (j,y), with j integer, and L(j,y)=0.
Let M=sum_(z integer)r(z)^d>0. The exact two centroid equations are

    sum_z (z-j) r(z)^d=0,
    sum_z d integral_0^(r(z)) t^(d-1)U(z,t)dt=0.       (3)

They are moment equations for the original uniform fiber measures.

Independently, vary the integer-coordinate tilt through the SAME point:

    H_v={L(z,x)+v dot(z-j)>=0},   v in R^n.

Then U_v(z,t)=U(z,t)+v dot(z-j). At a parameter where all partially
captured positive fibers have a differentiable inverse at their root
and there are no endpoint contacts, put

    beta_z=-partial_t U_v(z,c_z)>0,
    alpha_z=d c_z^(d-1)/beta_z.

The derivative of the mixed cap mass with respect to v is exactly

    sum_(proper z) (z-j) alpha_z.                     (4)

Implicit differentiation of U_v(z,c_z)=0 gives
partial_v c_z=(z-j)/beta_z, which proves (4). Equivalently,
alpha_z is the (d-1)-dimensional measure of the cut section divided by
||u||, by the coarea formula. Thus at a differentiable angular minimum,

    sum_(proper z) (z-j) alpha_z=0.                   (5)

These regularity hypotheses are stated, not inferred for every cap.
The integral identities (1)--(3) do not require them.

For d=1, after normalizing the continuous coefficient to one, each inverse
is U(z,t)=upper(z)-t. Therefore beta_z=1 and alpha_z=1 at every proper
fiber. When also n=1, (5) is the unweighted symmetric-block condition
used in the proved one-third integer-centroid theorem. In higher d the
beta_z generally differ, so replacing (5) by an unweighted sum loses the
actual section geometry.

The two centered laws in (3) and (5) have different weights. Joint
concavity of U is available, but no comparison in convex order between
these laws, no equality of beta_z, and no uniform simplex replacement is
proved or presumed here. Those would be additional mathematical steps.
